prompt: regex reference card please. the kind of thing you'd tape to your monitor

usability.notes: Exceptional desk reference. Flows naturally from foundations to advanced across two pages. RefRow gives a consistent 130px code column making sections trivially scannable. Code blocks appear judiciously for non-obvious examples without cluttering. Section 18 decision guide (spanning 3 cols) is a standout addition. Density is well-calibrated throughout. Minor redundancy in Section 12. Visual variety is high: RefRow, Code, Bullet, KV, Tag, and custom card grid all appear.

completeness.notes: Covers all core syntax, character classes, quantifiers, greedy/lazy, groups, lookarounds, flags, anchors. Dedicated JS and Python sections with full method APIs. Extras beyond the prompt: POSIX classes, copy-paste common patterns (email/URL/IPv4/date), substitution tokens, common pitfalls section, advanced PCRE constructs. Decision guide is unrequested but valuable. Only possible gap is Unicode property escapes (\p{}) but that is an edge case for a monitor reference. Depth is consistent across sections.

accuracy.notes: The cheatsheet is well-structured and mostly accurate, but contains two significant errors that would directly break user workflows: (1) The JavaScript named-group replacement syntax is shown as `${name}` when the correct MDN-specified syntax is `$<name>` — a user copying this would get a literal `${name}` string in their output. (2) Python's standard `re` module also requires fixed-width lookbehinds; only the third-party `regex` module lifts this restriction — the cheatsheet's claim that Python is an exception is incorrect and would mislead users. Additionally, `\w` is presented as strictly `[a-zA-Z0-9_]` without noting this is only true in ASCII/bytes mode — in default Unicode string mode it matches far more characters. The `matchAll` entry omits the mandatory `g`-flag requirement (a TypeError without it), which is a notable omission for a copy-paste reference. The remaining claims (metacharacters, anchors, `\Z`, POSIX classes, atomic group JS limitation, Python named group syntax, `\s` characters) are all accurate.

verified_claims.claim: JavaScript named group replacement syntax shown as `${name}` in the substitution patterns section
verified_claims.evidence: MDN documents the correct syntax as `$<name>` (angle brackets), not `${name}` (curly braces). Using `${name}` would produce a literal string rather than the captured group value. See: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/String/replace

Python's standard `re` module also requires fixed-width lookbehinds. Only the third-party `regex` module supports variable-length lookbehinds. The cheatsheet incorrectly lists Python alongside .NET as an exception to the fixed-width rule. See: https://docs.python.org/3/library/re.html and https://discuss.python.org/t/alternative-for-variable-length-lookbehind/24323

This is only true in bytes mode or when the `re.ASCII` flag is used. In default string mode, Python's `\w` matches all Unicode alphanumeric characters and underscore, which is a significantly broader set. Presenting it as simply `[a-zA-Z0-9_]` without qualification is misleading for a general-purpose reference. See: https://docs.python.org/3/library/re.html

verified_claims.claim: `str.matchAll(re)` described as 'Iterator of all match objects' with no mention of the `g` flag requirement
verified_claims.evidence: MDN states that `matchAll()` throws a TypeError if the regex does not have the global (`g`) flag set. Omitting this on a copy-paste reference card is a significant error — users will encounter an immediate runtime error. See: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/String/matchAll

verified_claims.claim: `\Z` matches absolute end of string in PCRE/Python
verified_claims.evidence: Confirmed by Python docs: `\Z` matches only at the very end of the string and is unaffected by `re.MULTILINE`. Also supported in PCRE2. See: https://docs.python.org/3/library/re.html
Confirmed as the correct Python-specific extension syntax in official Python documentation. See: https://docs.python.org/3/library/re.html

verified_claims.claim: Atomic groups `(?>...)` are not available in basic JavaScript
verified_claims.evidence: Confirmed by multiple sources including regular-expressions.info: JavaScript lacks native atomic grouping. The statement is accurate. See: https://www.regular-expressions.info/atomic.html

Confirmed by Python docs and standard regex references: `\s` matches space, tab, newline, carriage return, and form feed. The listed set is accurate for ASCII mode. See: https://docs.python.org/3/library/re.html
